newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish legislators back slower pensions growth.
newsitem.headline: Polish legislators back slower pensions growth.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament on Friday gave initial backing to a government bill curbing pension rises and sent it to committees for further analysis.

The bill, one of the first in a legislative package aimed at reforming Poland's inefficient social security system, would subject pension rises to annual negotiations and guarantee that they would not fall in real terms.
Deputies voted 310 to 65 with 18 abstentions against a motion to reject the draft law at its first reading.
Under the bill, pension increases would be negotiated in a special Trilateral Commission grouping representatives of the government, trade unions, employers and other organisations.
The result would be subject to parliament's decision each year during the budget debate, but would not be below the forecast growth of prices of a special basket of goods.
The present law, suspended for this year by a special bill securing 2.5-percent real pensions growth in 1996, pegs pensions' rise to average wage increases.
But the goverment argues the system could not be sustained as growth in real wages has been boosting budget subsidies to the social security system.
The new bill introduces two pension rises a year, in March and September, if annual inflation is higher than 10 percent, and only one, in June, if inflation falls below 10 percent.

The draft law, due to take effect next year, does not embrace the military, police and other uniformed services, which would be covered by a special bill to be worked out by 1998, Labour Minister Andrzej Baczkowski said last week.
Baczkowski said the bill, which will need to clear the senate and be signed by President Aleksander Kwasniewski, should guarantee a real pension increase of 1.5 percent next year.
He said on Thursday that real growth in pensions should reach four percent in 1997 because pensioners would also get a one-off payment stemming from a court ruling.
The constitutional court ruled earlier this year the government had to compensate pensioners for a rise they should have received to match pay rises in the last quarter of 1995.
